suggested.text:
My priorities are the ones this office actually controls: keeping city services staffed, defending our sanctuary ordinance against federal pressure, and building housing people who work here can afford.

I want to be direct about where I differ from the sitting Council. On June 23 they adopted the FY2027-28 budget unanimously — a budget SEIU 1021's own spokesperson called a flawed austerity plan, that laid off about 20 filled positions including six workers in one SEIU unit, and that shut down the Mobile Crisis Team after 46 years of city staffing. I would not have voted for it in that form.

Berkeley has a real structural deficit, roughly $29 million a year. That is not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether the first move is cutting the people who deliver services. It should be the last one.

The other priority is surveillance. Berkeley renewed its Flock license plate reader contract 5-4 in May, and that renewal lapses during the next term. Our own police audit found outside agencies entering "ICE" and "CBP" as their reason for searching data that included ours. A sanctuary ordinance the city cannot technically enforce is a promise we are not keeping.

questions.question: What public administration or leadership experience do you have? Please explain the programs you have developed and implemented for the benefit of the public.

suggested.text:
My experience is organizing, not administration, and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up.

When my coworkers at Berkeley Unified faced layoffs, I became the full-time organizer for AFT Local 6192 — the Berkeley Council of Classified Employees, roughly 600 people across nearly 100 classifications: clerical staff, special education instructional assistants, bus drivers. The same kinds of jobs SEIU represents at the City. I ran that campaign: the research, the one-on-ones, the turnout, the bargaining table.

That is directly relevant to how a councilmember should behave in a budget year. I know what it looks like when management presents a cut as inevitable and the numbers turn out to have room in them. I know the difference between meet-and-confer as a legal formality and as an actual process. And I know what a layoff does to a household, because I sat with people it happened to.

I also co-facilitate the Bay Resistance pod for the 94702 zip code, organizing neighbors around rapid response and immigration defense.

What I have not done is run a city department. I would lean on staff expertise and on the people doing the work, which is the same instinct that makes me want SEIU in the room early rather than late.

suggested.text:
Very few, and none of the ones usually offered.

Cost is not a sufficient reason. If a contractor is cheaper it is almost always because they pay less, staff thinner, or carry less liability, which means the savings are real for the budget and paid for by somebody's wages. That is a transfer, not an efficiency.

The circumstances I would consider: genuinely temporary surge capacity that does not recur; a specialized technical function the City has no realistic path to staffing, where no bargaining unit position is displaced; and work that is already regional by nature and better delivered jointly with other jurisdictions.

Even then I would want three things on the record before a vote: a true cost comparison that includes contract administration and oversight, the wage and benefit standard the contractor will be held to, and what happens when the contract ends.

Berkeley has just done the opposite of this. The Mobile Crisis Team, city staff since 1979, was eliminated and the function shifted to Alameda County while the county has its own budget problems. That was not a competitive procurement. It was a service being handed off under fiscal pressure, and I do not think Council examined it as the contracting-out decision it effectively was.

questions.question: In the event any public services were to be contracted out, would you support or oppose the requirement that the private contractor would have to offer its employees comparable wages and benefits?

suggested.text:
Support, without qualification.

If a private contractor takes over public work, they should be required to offer comparable wages and benefits. Otherwise the city is using its purchasing power to lower the standard in its own labor market — and Berkeley has spent decades doing the opposite. Our Living Wage Ordinance and Equal Benefits Ordinance already apply to city contractors. Extending comparability to any contracted-out public service is the same principle, applied where the pressure is greatest.

It also removes the incentive that drives most bad contracting decisions. When a contractor cannot win by paying less, the comparison becomes an honest one about capacity and quality, and most of the proposals that look attractive on a spreadsheet stop looking attractive.

I would want the requirement written with teeth: comparability defined against the relevant city classification rather than against a regional average, certified payroll, and a remedy the City will actually use. A standard nobody audits is a standard nobody meets.

I want to correct the premise gently, because it matters and because it is my own union.

Berkeley Unified's classified employees are not represented by SEIU. They are represented by the Berkeley Council of Classified Employees, AFT Local 6192 — about 600 people across nearly 100 classifications. I was their full-time organizer during the layoff fight.

So I can answer this from inside it. Part-time and temporary classified staff do the same work as permanent staff and are treated as a budget release valve. What they should have: proportional benefits rather than a cliff at an arbitrary hours threshold; real access to permanent openings, with internal candidates considered first; seniority that counts their actual service; and a limit on how long a position can be called temporary before it must be posted as permanent.

The instructional assistant working with special education students on a temporary designation for three consecutive years is not temporary. She is a permanent employee the district has declined to classify.

A councilmember does not set BUSD policy. What I can do is what I did as an organizer — show up, say this publicly, and back the local when it bargains.

questions.question: Many private companies receive public funds or other types of subsidies. Would you support or oppose requiring these private employers to remain neutral in union elections? Please explain your position.

suggested.text:
Support. If public money is going to a private employer, the public has a legitimate interest in how that employer treats the workers the subsidy helps pay for.

Neutrality is a modest ask. It does not require an employer to support a union. It requires them not to spend the workday, or the subsidy, campaigning against one. Captive audience meetings, one-on-one pressure from supervisors, and consultants hired to run an anti-union campaign are all things a company chooses to pay for — and when that company is receiving public funds, the public is indirectly paying for them.

Berkeley already conditions city contracts on labor standards through the Living Wage and Equal Benefits Ordinances. Attaching a neutrality expectation to discretionary subsidies, development agreements, and contracts is the same logic.

I would want it drafted carefully so it survives challenge — as a condition the City attaches to its own money rather than as a regulation of private labor relations, which is where preemption problems arise. I would rather have a narrower requirement that holds up than a broad one that gets enjoined.

I would start by making sure we are fighting the right measure, because the landscape has changed and a lot of the material in circulation is out of date.

questions.question: Please describe the circumstances under which you would support creation of any new tax preferences, i.e. tax “breaks”. What kinds of accountability would you require preventing abuse and how would you propose to pay for them?

suggested.text:
Rarely, and only where the alternative is worse.

The circumstances where I would consider one: a preference tied to something the market will not produce on its own and the city genuinely wants — deed-restricted affordable housing, or retaining a grocery or pharmacy in an underserved area. Not as a general incentive to attract business that would have come anyway.

The accountability I would require, written into the instrument rather than promised alongside it: a specific, measurable public benefit; a sunset date with no automatic renewal; clawback provisions that trigger on non-performance and that the City will actually enforce; annual public reporting of what the preference cost in foregone revenue against what it delivered; and labor standards, including prevailing or living wage and neutrality where applicable.

How to pay for it: by treating it as a budgeted expenditure rather than an invisible one. A tax break is spending. It should appear in the budget as a number, be reviewed on the same cycle as any other program, and compete against other uses of that money. Most tax preferences survive because nobody ever has to defend them again after the first vote.

By treating it as a standing function rather than something we do when a grant deadline appears.

Concretely: I would push for the City to maintain a real intergovernmental affairs capacity — someone whose actual job is tracking state and federal funding streams and building the relationships before the money is announced. Berkeley leaves money on the table because we are reactive, and small cities that invest one position in this consistently outperform their size.

That means two tracks at once — fight for every dollar through the ordinary channels, and simultaneously build local revenue that does not depend on a friendly administration. Berkeley already has the tools, and the honest answer is that enforcement is a resourcing question, not a legal one.

BMC 13.104 is our Wage Theft Prevention chapter, and the City's Labor Standards and Enforcement Program can investigate, access payroll records, and order corrective action, with penalties of $50 per day per affected employee. Publish outcomes — cases opened, wages recovered, employers cited — so the program is accountable and so the deterrent is real.

Partner with the worker centers and unions already finding these cases, and translate outreach into the languages of the workforce.

questions.question: What policies or actions will you support to address income inequality?

suggested.text:
The largest driver in Berkeley is housing cost, so most of what I would do about inequality is housing policy — a right to counsel for tenants facing eviction, TOPA so tenants can buy the buildings they live in, and enough new homes that vacancy stops being a bidding war.

On the wage side, Berkeley's minimum wage is $19.61 and indexed, which is real but not sufficient in this housing market. The bigger lever is union density. Nothing the City can do about wages by ordinance matches what a first contract does. So: neutrality conditions on subsidized employers, project labor and community workforce agreements where the City is spending, and using the seat publicly when workers organize.

And the City's own house. Berkeley employs about 1,600 people. The wages, benefits and job security we set are not a small intervention in the local economy — they are one of the largest single decisions this Council makes about inequality. A budget that lays off filled positions to close a structural gap is an inequality decision, whatever else it is called.

Progressive revenue is the third piece: taxing property, wealth and vacancy rather than sales, so the funding does not come back out of the same people.

suggested.text:
Three things a councilmember can actually do.

Start with the City as employer. Berkeley should run a pay equity audit across its own classifications and publish it — not just comparing men and women in the same job title, but examining whether historically women-dominated classifications are compensated below comparable male-dominated ones. That second question is where most of the municipal gap lives, and it is the one employers usually decline to ask. California's SB 1162 already requires pay data reporting from large employers; the City should hold itself to more than the minimum.

Second, the classifications themselves. Clerical, community services, library and instructional support are disproportionately women, and they are the classifications most exposed when a budget is balanced through attrition and part-time designations. Cutting there is a gendered decision even when nobody intends it as one.

Third, the conditions that make the gap stick: paid family leave beyond the state floor, predictable scheduling, and real access to promotion from part-time and temporary roles into permanent ones.

Outside the City, the strongest tool is the same as everywhere else — union contracts. Pay scales bargained transparently close gaps that individual negotiation reproduces.

suggested.text:
Yes, and specifically.

Public sector: bargain in good faith rather than through impasse; do not use vacancy elimination and temporary designations to shrink the unit without ever bargaining over it; and stop treating layoffs as the first structural tool. Berkeley SEIU members took a 99% strike authorization vote and noticed a citywide strike in November 2024. Whatever the merits of that dispute, a city that reaches strike notice with its own workforce has a management problem, not a labor problem.

Private sector: neutrality conditions on employers receiving city subsidies or contracts; project labor and community workforce agreements on city-funded construction; and Council resolutions supporting specific organizing drives, which cost nothing and matter more than people expect when workers are deciding whether the city is on their side.

And the part that is not policy. I will walk the picket line, speak at the rally, write the letter, and show up at the worksite. I did that as an organizer for AFT Local 6192 when Berkeley Unified classified staff faced layoffs. The reason I am comfortable committing to it is that I know what it is worth on the other end — which is real but limited, and no substitute for the votes.

questions.question: Will you support our union’s efforts to gain access to workers it does not have access to, so that workers have a meaningful opportunity to choose a union?

suggested.text:
Yes.

Where the City has authority, I would use it: access provisions in city contracts and leases, so that employers doing business with Berkeley cannot use city property to shut a union out; and the same condition attached to subsidies and development agreements. Public money should not buy an employer the ability to keep workers from hearing about a union.

For city employees, access should not be a fight at all. Reasonable worksite access, use of city facilities for meetings, new employee orientation time, and accurate contact information are all things the City can simply do well, and the fact that they periodically become disputes is itself a signal about how labor relations are being managed.

I would also say what I cannot do. A councilmember cannot compel a private employer with no city relationship to open its doors. What I can do is make it costly to be that employer in Berkeley — publicly, through the contracting relationship, and by showing up. That is a real tool but a bounded one, and I would rather tell you the boundary now than overpromise.

questions.question: Will you support the creation of alternative methods of aggregating workers’ power to change their work conditions and their communities, for example: allowing workers to create worker organizations, allowing payroll deductions, and the development of industry-wide wage, benefit, and work standards formed with worker input?

suggested.text:
Yes. The organizing framework built for a mid-century industrial workplace does not reach most of the people who need it now, and waiting for federal labor law reform is not a strategy.

The specific mechanisms in the question: I support allowing workers to form organizations that represent them without first winning a certification election; I support payroll deduction where the City is the employer or the contracting party, because the administrative burden is trivial and the barrier it removes is not; and I support sectoral and industry-wide standards developed with worker input, which is the model that has moved fastest in California — the Fast Food Council is the obvious example, and its wage floor did more for those workers than a decade of shop-by-shop campaigns.

At the city level the analogous tools are standards boards and workforce agreements that set conditions across an industry rather than one employer at a time, plus co-enforcement, where the City partners with worker organizations that can find violations the enforcement staff never will.

I would also want these built so they complement collective bargaining rather than substitute for it. A standards board is a floor. It is not a contract, and it should not be sold as one.

questions.question: Cost of living issues — name your solutions to addressing this issue.

suggested.text:
Two, and both are things this Council actually decides.

Housing. Rent is the cost driving everything else here. That means a right to counsel in eviction proceedings — Berkeley funds eviction defense at roughly $800,000 a year through Measure U1, which is a service that can run out mid-year rather than a right; TOPA, so tenants can buy their buildings, which Berkeley has never taken an up-or-down vote on; and enough new homes that vacancy stops being a bidding war. Berkeley is 37% of the way through its market-rate housing obligation and 6.5% through its very-low-income one. That gap is the cost-of-living story.

Wages and the public payroll. Berkeley's minimum wage is $19.61 and indexed, and the City employs about 1,600 people whose compensation is one of the largest single levers this Council has over the local cost of living. Protecting those jobs and those contracts is cost-of-living policy, not just labor policy.

The connection to your members is direct: your contract expires in June 2027, inside the next term. What the Council does about revenue between now and then determines what is on the table when you bargain.

suggested.text:
Berkeley has one of the strongest sanctuary policies in the country, and I would spend the term making sure it is enforceable rather than just declared.

The history is worth stating precisely, because it is frequently told wrong. Berkeley declared itself a City of Refuge in 1971 — Resolution 44,784-N.S. — but that was Vietnam-era, sheltering war resisters. The immigrant sanctuary commitment dates to 1986, Resolution 52,596-N.S., reaffirmed in 2007, 2015, 2016 and 2017. In September 2025 Council voted unanimously to move it from resolution into the municipal code, adding reporting requirements and a clearer prohibition on disclosing protected personal information. That shift from resolution to ordinance matters, because a resolution is a statement and an ordinance is law.

Our policy has no criminal carve-out, and I would defend that. A carve-out is not a narrow exception in practice; it is a reason for every immigrant in the city to assume that calling the police is a risk.

The unfinished piece is technical. Berkeley operates automated license plate readers whose data has been searched by outside agencies citing ICE and CBP. A sanctuary ordinance the city cannot technically enforce is a promise we are not keeping. That contract lapses next term.

Audit the data. Districts and cities collect more than they realize, and vendor contracts are where it leaks. Every system holding student or family data should be reviewed for what it shares, with whom, and under what legal process.

suggested.text:
Two things.

The first is that I am not going to tell you I have always agreed with this Council. I would not have voted for the June budget in the form it passed. I understand the constraint — roughly $29 million a year, structural, papered over with one-time moves until there was nothing left to paper with. But the sequence mattered. Your members were brought in after the framework was set, and the vote was unanimous anyway. If you endorse me you are getting someone who will say that out loud on the dais, including when it is uncomfortable and including to people I otherwise agree with.

The second is that my labor background is AFT, not SEIU — Local 6192, the classified employees at Berkeley Unified, where I was the full-time organizer during the layoff fight. Different union, same work: clerical, instructional support, transportation, the people who keep an institution running and get called overhead in a budget document.

Your contract expires in June 2027, inside the next term. I would rather you know now exactly what I think about how the last budget was made than find out during bargaining.
